subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: adding a checklist and guardrail [Action]
passage:
Kunal, come and sit. You joined after the night of the big outage, so let me tell you what came after. I'm Omkar.
Farah, one of our juniors, had run a delete command against the live data instead of the test copy. The first hour was chaos. After we got it back, my instinct was to write "be careful" on a slide and move on. Then I asked, what would stop the next person? Anyone.
So we did three plain things. Any command that deletes now needs a second person's OK. Test and live logins are separate, with different passwords. And we wrote a short checklist on one page and pinned it to the wall.
Farah read the checklist twice, and smiled for the first time in a week.

qa.q: What did Farah run the delete command against by mistake?
qa.a: Farah ran it against the live data instead of the test copy.

qa.q: What was Farah probably feeling after the outage?
qa.a: Farah was ashamed and weighed down, since the smile a week later was the first sign of relief.

qa.q: Omkar's team added a second person's OK, separate logins and a checklist. What did that choice do?
qa.a: It made the safeguards part of the system, so the same slip could not repeat, whoever was working.

qa.q: How might Farah have felt on reading the checklist?
qa.a: Farah probably felt relief and reassurance that the team fixed the set-up instead of blaming a person, which is why the first smile came.

grounding: The elder's story shows a team adding a review for deleting commands, separating test and live logins and writing a short checklist so the same slip cannot repeat.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: adding a checklist and guardrail [Action]
passage:
Two days after Jeevan's command wiped a staging table that turned out to feed production, the client wanted the next release by Friday. Vidya, the team lead, could have said, 'Be more careful,' and shipped. Instead she blocked two hours on Wednesday, deadline or not.
They made three changes. First, any command that deletes or drops data now needed a second engineer's approval in the tool before it could run. Second, test and production credentials were split; Jeevan's laptop could no longer reach production at all without a separate login. Third, a five-line checklist was pinned in the team channel: which server, which account, backup confirmed, reviewer named, time noted.
The release went out on Friday evening, an hour late. On Monday, a new intern tried a drop command. The tool stopped it and asked for a reviewer.

qa.q: What was the first change the team made?
qa.a: Any command that deletes or drops data now needed a second engineer's approval in the tool before it could run.

qa.q: Why did Vidya take two hours despite the deadline, and what was she likely worried about?
qa.a: She was worried the same slip could happen again, and felt that 'be more careful' alone would not protect the team.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep the checklist from being ignored?
qa.a: They could build the checklist steps into the tool itself and look at near misses together each month, so it stays part of the work.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel about the new guardrails?
qa.a: Jeevan may feel relieved that the fix is about the system, not a judgement on Jeevan alone.

grounding: It shows a team adding a required review for destructive commands, separate credentials and a short checklist so the same slip cannot repeat.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: adding a checklist and guardrail [Action]
passage:
In the Hitec City office, Yogesh pinned a single page above the team's shared desk. The Tuesday before, Ritu had run a bulk refund script meant for the test system on the live one, and 212 customers got refunds they hadn't asked for. It took the whole week to recover.
Yogesh didn't give a speech about carefulness. He changed things. The refund tool now asked for a second person's approval before any bulk action. Test and live logins were split: different passwords, and the live screen turned red. And the page above the desk was a checklist: 'Which system? Which login? How many rows? Who reviewed? Backup taken?'
Ritu read it twice. 'Would this have stopped me?'
'At step one,' Yogesh said. 'The screen would have been red.'

qa.q: How many customers got refunds they hadn't asked for?
What might Ritu have been feeling on asking 'Would this have stopped me?'
qa.a: Ritu probably still felt guilty and anxious, hoping the new setup would prevent a repeat and that the fault wasn't Ritu's alone.

qa.q: Which change is most likely to stop the same slip, and why?
qa.a: Splitting the logins and turning the live screen red, because it makes the wrong system obvious before anything runs.

qa.q: How might customers be affected by these guardrails in future?
qa.a: They are less likely to face confusing refunds and follow-up calls, so their trust in the company holds.

grounding: It shows a team adding a second approval for bulk actions, separate test and live logins and a short checklist so the same slip cannot happen again.
